strengths: Novel theoretical framework extending diffusion wavelets to vector-valued signals with proven SE(3)-equivariance via local SVD-based coordinate systems
Strong theoretical guarantees: frame bounds (Theorem 3.1) and equivariance properties (Theorems 3.2-3.3) with detailed rigorous proofs
Impressive parameter efficiency: achieves comparable performance to EGNN with 59,779 parameters vs. 284,036 (79% reduction) and vs. TFN with 99.8% fewer parameters
Clear demonstration of equivariance importance through test set rotation experiments showing dramatic failure of non-equivariant variants
Avoids oversmoothing problem of message-passing networks through single-layer multiscale feature extraction
Comprehensive technical documentation: detailed proofs, architectural specifications, complexity analysis supporting reproducibility
weaknesses: Critical limitation: experiments exclusively on synthetic data (random ellipsoids with 512 graphs of 128 nodes). No real-world validation on molecular, protein, or other standard benchmarks where geometric equivariance is practically important

Insufficient exploration of design choices: no ablation studies on Gaussian kernel scale ϵ, minimum degree requirement (ni ≥ d), or SVD degeneracy assumptions; robustness of sign-flipping procedure not empirically validated
Frame bounds depend on dmin/dmax singular value ratio with no analysis of performance on irregular graphs where this ratio is unfavorable

Restrictive activation function constraint requiring σ to commute with rotations (Theorem 3.3); while constructible, standard activations (ReLU, tanh) don't satisfy this, limiting practical flexibility
Graph modification requirement: enforcing ni ≥ d by adding edges alters graph structure in ways that could affect structure-sensitive tasks; impact not explored
Limited baseline comparisons: missing recent equivariant methods (NequIP, Allegro, etc.) and other equivariant scattering approaches mentioned in related work

Gap between theory and implementation: method uses non-dyadic InfoGain-selected wavelets, removes nonlinearity from scattering coefficients, adds Dirac features—modifications not formally justified despite claims theoretical guarantees adapt
Incomplete complexity analysis: O(d∑ki²) SVD cost per node could be prohibitive for large-degree nodes; no empirical scaling analysis beyond wall-clock timing

strengths: Mathematically sound theory with rigorous proofs of equivariance (Theorems 3.2-3.3) and frame bounds (Theorem 3.1)
Achieves comparable performance to EGNN and TFN with dramatically fewer parameters (59,779 vs. 29M for TFN)
Novel extension of geometric scattering to vector-valued node features with SO(d)-equivariance guarantees
Well-organized presentation with comprehensive appendices including detailed proofs and implementation details
Effective visual illustrations of rotational equivariance (Figures 1-2)
weaknesses: Critical limitation: Experiments exclusively on synthetic toy problems (ellipsoid diameter prediction, surface normal functions). Zero validation on standard benchmarks (QM9, OC20, MD-17) or real molecular graphs despite motivation for such applications. This is disqualifying for ICML standards.

Significant gap between theory and practice: Implementation uses generalized wavelets (P^{t_j-1} - P^{t_j}), no non-linearity in scattering, and InfoGain scale selection, diverging from dyadic wavelets in theory. Claims theoretical guarantees 'readily adapt' without justification. Equivariance guarantees' applicability to the actual implementation is unclear.

Unclear practical advantages: Comparable (not superior) performance to EGNN/TFN, with parameter efficiency as secondary benefit. No evidence of scalability beyond 128-point graphs. Table 1 shows non-equivariant version has 100× worse validation error, suggesting artificial test design (rotating only test set, not validation). When would practitioners use this method over existing approaches?

Limited technical novelty: Primarily combines existing techniques (geometric scattering, vector diffusion maps, equivariant GNNs). Insufficient differentiation from concurrent work (Chew et al. 2022, 2024; Johnson et al. 2025a) on geometric scattering for geometric graphs.

Restrictive and unanalyzed assumptions: Theorem 3.3 requires activation function commutativity with rotations; practical implications unexplored. Kernel scale ε selection appears ad-hoc without sensitivity analysis. Frame bound dependencies on degree ratio (d_min/d_max) not discussed. SVD sign-flipping solution (Appendix C) is unprincipled with unstated computational costs.

Missing critical ablations and analyses: Why is non-equivariant variant so much worse? Sensitivity to hyperparameters (ε, scales)? Computational scalability with graph size and node degree? No comparison with other scattering GNNs (Min et al., Tong et al., Johnson et al.).

Incomplete experimental setup: Small scale (512 graphs, 128 points, ~100 per test fold via 5-fold CV). Ellipsoid construction artificially designed to favor equivariance (rotation only test set). Missing code availability link. No discussion of when method is not appropriate.
Reproducibility concerns: Implementation deviates substantially from theory without clear documentation of impact. Many hyperparameter choices lack justification or sensitivity analysis.

strengths: Rigorous theoretical framework with complete proofs of frame bounds and rotational equivariance properties for vector diffusion wavelets
Novel methodological contribution combining vector diffusion maps with scattering transforms through SVD-based local coordinate systems
Significant parameter efficiency: ESc-GNN achieves 59K parameters vs 284K for EGNN and 29M for TFN while maintaining comparable accuracy
Clear demonstration of equivariance importance: non-equivariant models fail catastrophically on rotated test data (validation MSE 0.3126 vs test MSE 2.9181)
Well-organized presentation with comprehensive appendices, clear notation, illustrative figures, and thorough hyperparameter documentation
Proper treatment of implementation details including SVD sign-ambiguity resolution and detailed complexity analysis
weaknesses: Experiments limited exclusively to synthetic data (randomly sampled ellipsoids); no validation on standard real-world benchmarks (QM9, MD17, OC20, molecular graphs)

Significant gap between theory and practice: theory uses no nonlinearity in wavelets, but implementation uses nonlinearities differently via InfoGain wavelets and gating functions—unclear if Theorem 3.3 applies to actual implementation
Title claims SE(3)-equivariance but paper only proves SO(d)-equivariance (rotations only, not translations)—this is mathematically misleading as SE(3) includes translations
Competitive advantage is primarily parameter efficiency, not accuracy: on node-level task (Table 2) TFN achieves 0.1145 MSE vs. ESc-GNN's 0.1513—TFN significantly outperforms
Theorem 3.3 requires restrictive activation function assumption (σ(R·w) = R·σ(w)); proposed radial activation solution limits expressiveness with no capacity analysis
Small synthetic datasets (512 graphs, 128 points) with simple tasks (diameter prediction, bandlimited functions) do not convincingly demonstrate utility for real applications
Missing comparisons with other parameter-efficient equivariant methods; unclear when practitioners should adopt this approach over existing alternatives
Ad-hoc implementation choices (Dirac delta node features) lack theoretical motivation and create additional gap between theory and practice
No evaluation on molecular graphs, point clouds, or other standard geometric deep learning benchmarks despite claimed applications
Insufficient ablation studies: decomposition of efficiency gains across architecture components not provided

strengths: Rigorous theoretical analysis with proven frame bounds and rotational equivariance properties (Theorems 3.1-3.3)
Significant parameter efficiency gains compared to baselines (20K-60K vs 300K-29M parameters), with practical benefits for deployment
Comprehensive experimental validation across three diverse domains (synthetic, wind, neural data) with proper cross-validation and statistical testing
Well-designed ablation studies clearly demonstrating the importance of equivariance (Table 1 shows dramatic failure of non-equivariant models under rotation)
Natural extension from scalar diffusion wavelets with clear motivation from vector diffusion maps and principled mathematical framework
Excellent presentation with effective visualizations (Figures 3-4) and detailed appendices supporting reproducibility
Automatic translation invariance and thorough computational complexity analysis
weaknesses: Marginal or absent empirical improvements: wind task shows VDW-GNN (2.75 MSE) statistically indistinguishable from EGNN (2.77 MSE), neural task shows no significant difference vs MARBLE (p > 0.05)
Limited novelty: extending scalar to vector wavelets via local SVD-based rotations is straightforward; frame bounds result is expected given orthogonal transformation properties
Unclear practical guidance: paper fails to identify when VDW-GNNs should be preferred over simpler equivariant methods (EGNN, TFN)
Restrictive activation function requirement (Theorem 3.3): activation must commute with rotations, limiting architectural flexibility with suggested radial function solution
Suspicious baseline comparison: DD-TNN performs catastrophically worse (12.76 vs 2.75 MSE) with no explanation, raising questions about fair comparison or setup bias favoring VDW-GNN

Arbitrary graph construction choices: k-NN graphs lack sensitivity analysis; artificial edge addition when deg(vi) < D could affect geometric validity; wind experiment uses artificial directional edges
Primary advantage is parameter efficiency rather than predictive accuracy, providing limited motivation for adoption in modern deep learning where memory is less constrained than accuracy
Incomplete reproducibility: code URL missing; many hyperparameter choices appear ad-hoc; InfoGain wavelets procedure adds undocumented complexity
Limited scope of real-world experiments: small graphs (≤2000 nodes); neural data uses derived velocity features rather than raw signals; scalability to large graphs not addressed
Frame bounds result lacks practical context: connection between tighter bounds and generalization performance is not established; implications for learning unclear

strengths: Solid mathematical framework with rigorous proofs of frame bounds (Theorem 3.1) and rotational equivariance (Theorems 3.2-3.3) for vector diffusion wavelets
Well-motivated approach addressing the oversmoothing vs. underreaching tradeoff in GNNs through geometric perspective on manifolds
Computational efficiency: 57-59K parameters vs. 284K-29M for EGNN/TFN with sparse matrix operations
Comprehensive experimental methodology including 5-fold CV, multiple baselines, inductive evaluation on neural data, and extensive reproducibility details
Clear mathematical exposition and technical soundness of core derivations
weaknesses: Incremental core contribution: extending diffusion wavelets to vector-valued signals via SVD-based local coordinates and Singer & Wu (2012) is a straightforward engineering application rather than fundamental innovation

Weak primary empirical result: neural data experiment (main real-world validation) shows 66% vs 65% MARBLE accuracy with explicit statement that distributions are 'not significantly different under a two-sided Wilcoxon test,' contradicting the empirical contribution

No clear practical advantage demonstrated: outperforms on parameter efficiency but not prediction performance; unclear when to use VDW-GNNs over EGNN/TFN for equivariance or standard methods for general tasks

Significant theory-practice misalignment: theory assumes dyadic wavelets but experiments use non-dyadic scales via InfoGain procedure; activation functions must commute with rotations (restrictive) but implementation choices unclear

Narrow experimental scope with questionable design: ellipsoids rotation adversarially constructed for equivariance testing; wind improvements marginal without significance testing; no experiments with high-dimensional vector features (D >> 3)

Technical concerns inadequately addressed: method requires n_i ≥ D neighbors (limiting), frame bounds contain d_max/d_min ratio (unbounded), O(D³) computational terms contradict efficiency claims, sign-flipping procedure (Appendix C) is ad-hoc and lacks theoretical justification
Missing ablation studies: no decomposition of contributions from vector equivariance vs. scattering vs. parameter efficiency; no comparison of SVD-based vs. learnable coordinate systems
Statistical rigor lacking: most results lack significance testing; neural data result explicitly shows null effect but presented as success; wind field improvements lack error bars

strengths: Novel theoretical contribution extending diffusion wavelets to vector-valued node features with rigorous proofs of frame bounds (Theorem 3.1) and rotational equivariance (Theorems 3.2-3.3)
Demonstrated computational efficiency with substantially fewer parameters than EGNN and TFN baselines while maintaining competitive performance (e.g., 59,779 vs 284,036 parameters on ellipsoid task)
Thoughtful experimental design including clever rotation-based test for equivariance on synthetic data and more rigorous inductive evaluation protocol on neural data
Thorough documentation of all experimental details, hyperparameters, and architectural choices enabling reproducibility
Well-grounded motivation connecting vector diffusion maps, connection Laplacian, and manifold learning with clear presentation and effective visualizations
weaknesses: Neural data experiments (main real-world validation) show statistically insignificant improvement over MARBLE (66% vs 65%, p > 0.05), undermining practical utility claims despite better efficiency
Restrictive activation function requirement (σ must commute with rotations, excluding standard ReLU) for Theorem 3.3 is not prominently discussed despite being significant limitation
Limited experimental scope: modest graph sizes (max 2000 nodes), only three specialized application domains, no evaluation on standard GNN benchmarks, missing scalability analysis
Incomplete comparison with DD-TNN (designed for tangent bundle data): dramatic performance difference (MSE 12.76 vs 2.75) confounded by different graph construction (masked edges in modified setup)

Insufficient ablation studies and design justification: architecture choices (gating, mixing, Dirac features) lack clear motivation; sensitivity to kernel parameter ε not analyzed; impact of requiring n_i ≥ D not studied
Frame bounds depend on degree ratio (d_min/d_max), potentially very loose for irregular graphs common in practice; manifold vs. general GNN leverage unclear
Dependency on concurrent unpublished work (InfoGain wavelets, Johnson et al. 2025b) for non-dyadic scales reduces self-containment
